content: Tabebuia is a genus of neotropical plants that includes approximately 100 species within the tribe Tecomeae of the family Bignoniaceae. These species are distributed from northern Mexico and the Antilles down to northern Argentina, including the islands of Hispaniola (comprising the Dominican Republic and Haiti) and Cuba. Description Tabebuia species are large shrubs or trees that can grow to heights ranging from 5 to 50 meters (16 to 160 feet), depending on the species. Many of these species are deciduous during the dry season, while others are evergreen. The leaves are arranged in opposite pairs and can be either simple or palmately compound, typically consisting of 3 to 7 leaflets. Tabebuia is particularly notable for its striking flowers. The flowers are 3 to 11 cm (1 to 4 inches) wide and are produced in dense clusters. The calyx of the flowers is cup-shaped and can vary in form, being campanulate, tubular, truncate, bilabiate, or five-lobed. The corolla colors differ between species and may include white, light pink, yellow, lavender, magenta, or red. The outer texture of the flower tube can be either smooth (glabrous) or covered with fine hairs (pubescent). The fruit of Tabebuia is a dehiscent pod, measuring 10 to 50 cm (4 to 20 inches) in length, and contains numerous seeds, some of which are winged. These pods often remain on the tree throughout the dry season and are shed at the onset of the rainy season. Usage Several species within the Tabebuia genus are valued as timber trees. The wood is commonly used for furniture, decking, and other outdoor applications due to its durability and resistance to insects. It has a fire rating of A1, the highest possible rating, comparable to concrete, and is denser than water, causing it to sink. Tabebuia wood, particularly FSC-certified ipe wood, has become increasingly popular as a decking material because of its insect resistance and longevity. Tabebuia trees are also widely used as ornamental plants in landscaping, public squares, and boulevards due to their vibrant and colorful flowers. The flowers often bloom on leafless stems at the end of the dry season, making the floral display even more prominent. The bark of certain Tabebuia species, especially the inner bark of Tabebuia impetiginosa (commonly known as Lapacho or Taheebo), has medicinal uses. The primary active compounds in the bark include lapachol, quercetin, and other flavonoids. The inner bark is dried, shredded, and boiled to produce a bitter or sour-tasting tea with a brownish color. This tea is also available in pill form. It is traditionally used during flu and cold seasons and is believed to alleviate smoker's cough by acting as an expectorant, helping to expel deeply embedded mucus and contaminants from the lungs. Additionally, some Tabebuia species are used as an additive in certain versions of the psychedelic drink Ayahuasca. Notable Species Among the nearly 100 species of Tabebuia, some notable examples include: Tabebuia alba: Native to Brazil, also known as Tecoma alba or Handroanthus albus. Tabebuia caraiba: Found in Brazil, with several synonyms such as Tecoma argentea and Handroanthus caraiba. Tabebuia chrysantha: Known as Araguaney in northern South America, it is the national tree of Venezuela. Its flowers are yellow, and in northern Colombia, it is referred to as Cañaguate. Tabebuia chrysotricha: Commonly called the Golden Trumpet Tree, it is native to Brazil and produces golden-yellow to red flowers. Tabebuia donnell-smithii: Known as Prima Vera or Gold Tree, it is native to Mexico and Central America. This species is considered one of the most colorful trees in Central America, with masses of golden-yellow flowers that cover the crown after the leaves are shed. Tabebuia impetiginosa: Also known as Pink Ipe or Lapacho, it is native to South America, particularly Brazil. Its bark is used medicinally, and it is a popular street tree in tropical cities due to its light pink flowers and modest size. Tabebuia serratifolia: Known as Yellow Poui or Ipe, it is a commercially farmed hardwood notable for its extreme hardness and resistance to fire and pests. Its inner bark is used to treat fungal infections. Exploitation The demand for ipe wood, derived from Tabebuia species, has risen significantly in recent years, particularly in the United States. By the 1990s, environmental organizations working to preserve the Amazon Rainforest reported that approximately 80% of logging in the Brazilian Amazon was illegal. This was later confirmed by the Brazilian government, including a leaked report from the Brazilian Intelligence Agency (SAE), which revealed that five times the amount of wood legally sanctioned for logging was being exported. The report also implicated numerous staff members of the environmental agency IBAMA in accepting bribes. A Greenpeace report titled The Santarém Five and Illegal Logging — A Case Study highlighted five companies involved in illegal logging in the Santarém region of Pará. At the time, exports from this region were primarily destined for the Netherlands and France, with ipe wood being among the illegal exports. Much of the ipe wood imported into the United States is used for decking. Starting in the late 1960s, importing companies targeted large boardwalk projects to sell ipe wood, beginning with New York City Parks and Recreation. The city began using ipe wood for its boardwalks, including the one along Coney Island Beach, and eventually converted the entire 10-mile (16-km) boardwalk to ipe. The wood lasted approximately 25 years, after which it was replaced with new ipe in 1994. Given that ipe trees typically grow at densities of only one or two trees per acre, vast areas of forest must be logged to meet the demand for boardwalks and, to a lesser extent, homeowner decks. For New York City’s 10 miles of boardwalk, an estimated 83,360 acres (337 km²) of Amazon rainforest would need to be logged.
